extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of comedy/SNL; aspiring comedians interested in topical/roast humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria for creating short, topical, roast-style jokes aimed at public figures (as exemplified by Norm Macdonald's Weekend Update material and the consequences he faced). Focuses on punchlines, topicality, edginess, repetition, and navigating institutional/political constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Making fun of a public figure can be more or less controversial depending on current public sentiment; the article states 'making fun of OJ isn’t exactly controversial these days.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use current public opinion to judge acceptability—targets widely perceived as culpable or disgraceful may be safer subjects for ridicule. However, timing and cultural context matter; what feels acceptable now may have been more sensitive at the time (the piece discusses Norm's jokes in the 1990s vs today's views).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline-driven one-liners
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, tightly constructed one-liners with an unexpected twist or juxtaposition are a core technique (exemplified by Norm's lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: 'that is some bad luck when the one guy who would have died for you, kills you.'; 'sleepy truckers are responsible for 1,000 deaths a year. In second place, OJ Simpson at two deaths a year.'; 'There it is, I’ve been looking all over for that thing!' Use concise setups that lead to a sharp, surprising payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark humor and irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Using dark subject matter (murder, bloody evidence) and ironic framing to produce laughs is part of the comic approach shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights jokes that invoke the bloody glove and the notion of someone who 'would have died for you, kills you.' Dark irony can be effective but inherently risky; expect stronger reactions and possible institutional pushback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition/target fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly targeting the same person or topic ('he simply would not stop making fun of OJ Simpson') can provoke backlash beyond typical audience reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse of a single target; even successful bits can lead to friction with decision-makers or audience fatigue if they are perceived as obsessive rather than varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and personal-political constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Network executives' relationships and sensibilities influence what material gets tolerated—Norm was allegedly removed because Don Ohlmeyer, a friend/supporter of OJ, was offended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate gatekeepers' loyalties and potential censorship. Even if material plays to audiences, personal relationships and corporate politics can limit a comedian's platform (e.g., demotion, removal, bans on promotional material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance role matters (segment persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform/role (e.g., Weekend Update host vs. regular cast member) shapes both what material is expected and what liberty a performer has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As host of a news-parody segment, Norm's biting topical jokes were more prominent; removal from that role reduced his influence and visibility. Consider how your bit fits the persona/segment you're performing in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning career setbacks into material
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics can and do use professional setbacks or conflicts as fodder for later jokes ('I haven’t gotten funnier, the show has gotten really bad!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe dismissals or controversies into self-aware or retaliatory jokes when appropriate—this can restore agency and generate new material, but timing and tone are important to avoid seeming bitter rather than funny.
